title: Fame, Fortune, and Murder in 1960s France
gist: Marie Le Conte reviews Edward Chisholm's Murder in Paris '68, about the unsolved 1968 killing of Stevan Markovic, an associate of actor Alain Delon, which became a political scandal touching Prime Minister Georges Pompidou. She credits the book's portrait of postwar France but argues Chisholm overstates its grand meaning: Markovic may simply have been a minor crook.

insights.claim: Stevan Markovic, a Yugoslav associate of Alain Delon, was found dead in 1968; before his death he wrote that Delon would be '10,000% responsible' if anything happened to him, and the murder was never solved.
insights.speaker: Marie Le Conte

insights.claim: Chisholm identifies four theories of the murder: revenge for an affair with Delon's wife, preventing sale of compromising stories, underworld dealings, or knowledge of elite secrets, with gangster François Marcantoni central to most.

insights.claim: Postwar France of the 1950s-60s was still shaped by Nazi occupation and Vichy collaboration, with Resistance veterans like Marcantoni moving between underworld and establishment.
insights.speaker: Marie Le Conte
insights.so_what: Context on persistent wartime legacies in French politics.

insights.claim: Pompidou's succession after de Gaulle's 1969 resignation marked France turning toward the future, while Delon's support for de Gaulle positioned him with the old guard.
insights.speaker: Marie Le Conte

insights.claim: Le Conte argues Chisholm overreaches in framing the affair as a story about power and all of human life; Markovic may just have been a minor crook who died as minor crooks did.
insights.speaker: Marie Le Conte
insights.so_what: A caution against over-narrativizing scandals into grand theses.
